title: How to Write a Winning Public Sector Bid
author_bio: Philip has over 24 years of recruitment experience and has provided specialist bid, proposal and tender writing services for the last 14 years, across frameworks including Crown Commercial Service, Workforce Alliance and HTE.
excerpt: After fourteen years writing and reviewing tenders, the same handful of things separate a bid that scores well from one that quietly comes last, and almost none of it has to do with how good the business actually is.
body:
I've read more losing bids than winning ones. That's not a boast, it's just the nature of the job. After fourteen years writing tenders and reviewing other people's, you start to notice the same handful of things separating a bid that scores well from one that quietly comes last, and almost none of it has to do with how good the business actually is.

Most of the companies I've worked with over the years were perfectly capable of delivering the contract. Some of them were better than the supplier who eventually won. What they weren't always good at was writing a document that proved it to someone who has never met them and never will.

Start with the scoring matrix, not the question

Every tender comes with a breakdown of how marks are awarded, and most people skim it once and then go straight to writing. Read it properly first. If quality is worth 70 percent and price is worth 30, that tells you where your effort needs to go. If a single question is worth 15 percent of the entire submission, that question deserves more than a paragraph lifted from last year's bid.

I still see businesses write a beautifully polished answer to a question nobody asked, because it's the answer they're proud of, not the one the buyer wants. The evaluator isn't grading your company. They're grading how precisely your answer matches their mark scheme. Those are not the same exercise.

Answer the actual question

This sounds obvious until you read a few hundred submissions. A buyer asks how you'll manage staff turnover on a contract and gets back three paragraphs about the company's general training philosophy. It's not wrong information, it's just not an answer. If the question has three parts, answer all three, in order, and make it easy for the evaluator to find each one.

A trick that helps more than people expect: lift the question's own language back into your answer. If they ask about "continuity of service during staff absence," use that exact phrase early in your response. Evaluators are often scoring dozens of submissions against a checklist, and a response that visibly tracks the question gets read more carefully than one that makes them hunt for the relevant bit.

Evidence beats confidence

"We have a highly experienced team" tells the evaluator nothing they can score. "Our account managers have an average of nine years in public sector recruitment, and we retained 94 percent of placed staff on our last NHS framework contract" tells them something specific, checkable, and comparable to the next supplier's answer.

If you don't have a strong number for something, say so honestly and explain what you do instead. A specific, modest claim backed by evidence will always outscore a vague, impressive sounding one. Evaluators have seen enough generic bids to be suspicious of confidence that isn't backed up.

Build one consistent story, not twelve separate answers

The strongest bids read like they were written by one person with one clear argument for why this supplier is the right choice, even when six different people contributed sections. Decide early what your two or three win themes are, the real reasons you're a good fit for this specific contract, and make sure they show up consistently across the document rather than being buried in one answer and absent from the rest.

Compliance is how you lose without ever being scored

Every year I see a genuinely strong submission disqualified for something that had nothing to do with the quality of the writing. A missing attachment. A word count ignored. A document uploaded to the wrong portal section five minutes after the deadline. None of that gets you marked down, it gets you removed from consideration entirely, and no amount of good writing afterward changes that.

Build in time at the end specifically for a compliance check against the instructions document, done by someone who hasn't been staring at the bid for two weeks and has gone slightly blind to it.

The businesses that win aren't always the best ones

They're the ones who treated the written response as seriously as the service they're actually offering. That's the part I'd want any business new to tendering to take away from this. The work you do and the bid you write are two different disciplines, and getting good at the second one is entirely learnable, it just takes someone willing to read the scoring criteria properly and resist the urge to write the answer they'd rather give.

If you want a second pair of eyes on a live tender before you submit it, that's exactly what we're here for.

title: A Guide to G-Cloud 14 for IT Consultancies
author_bio: James leads business development and bid management at Hawkeye Solutions, with particular success across G-Cloud and Digital Outcomes and Specialists frameworks, helping IT consultancies win public sector contracts.
excerpt: Getting onto G-Cloud is the easy part. Winning work through it is where most IT consultancies either get it right, or waste a listing that never earns them a single call-off.
body:
Every few months someone asks me the same question: should we get onto G-Cloud? The honest answer is usually yes, but with a caveat nobody tells you upfront, which is that getting on the framework is the easy part. Winning work through it is where most IT consultancies either get it right or waste a listing that never earns them a single call-off.

What G-Cloud actually is

G-Cloud is a Crown Commercial Service framework that lets public sector buyers, central government, NHS trusts, local authorities, buy cloud services without running a full open tender for every purchase. Instead, approved suppliers list their services on the Digital Marketplace, and buyers either browse and award directly for smaller purchases or run a short mini-competition between a handful of suppliers for bigger ones.

It renews roughly every two years. G-Cloud 14 is the current iteration, and if you're reading this after a new version has launched, the structure and the advice below will still largely hold, the framework gets refreshed more than it gets reinvented.

The three lots, in plain terms

G-Cloud splits into three categories, and most consultancies only genuinely belong in one or two of them.

  • Lot 1, Cloud Hosting. Infrastructure and platform services: compute, storage, hosting environments. If you're a hosting or infrastructure provider, this is you.
  • Lot 2, Cloud Software. Software as a service, applications buyers can procure directly. This is the most competitive lot by volume of listings.
  • Lot 3, Cloud Support. The one most IT consultancies actually belong in: implementation, migration, ongoing support, and specialist cloud services. If you help organisations plan, build or run cloud systems rather than selling the infrastructure itself, this is your lot.

Getting this right matters because buyers search by lot and by category tags within it. List yourself under the wrong one and you're invisible to the people actually looking for what you do.

Applying isn't a tender, but treat it like one anyway

The application window is short, usually a few weeks, and it opens roughly every two years rather than on demand. You'll need to evidence your company's financial standing, provide service descriptions for everything you're listing, and set your pricing. None of it is scored competitively in the way a normal tender is: if you meet the standard, you're in. But the quality of what you write at this stage determines whether anyone finds you once you are.

Write your service descriptions the way you'd write marketing copy aimed at a time-pressed procurement officer, not the way you'd write an internal capability document. Specific, plain, and focused on the outcome a buyer gets, not the technology stack you're proud of.

Where the real competition happens

Being on G-Cloud gets you a listing. It doesn't get you work. Buyers find suppliers two ways: direct award, where they search the marketplace and pick a supplier whose listing answers their need clearly enough to award without further competition, and mini-competitions, where a shortlist of suppliers is invited to respond to a short brief, often with a tight turnaround of a week or two.

The direct award route rewards clarity. A listing that's vague about what you actually do, or buried in jargon, simply won't come up in the searches that matter. The mini-competition route rewards speed and preparation: have case studies, pricing structures and reference material ready to go before the invitation lands, because a two-week turnaround doesn't leave room to start from scratch.

The mistakes I see most often

Consultancies list themselves once and never touch it again. Service descriptions written two years ago, pricing that's drifted out of date, no case studies added even after winning real contracts through the framework. A stale listing looks exactly like an inactive supplier to a buyer browsing the marketplace, and they move on to the next one.

The other common mistake is pricing too cautiously out of fear of looking expensive, then discovering the day rate doesn't cover the actual cost of delivery once a mini-competition is won. Price for the work you'd actually want to do, not the lowest number that might win something.

Why it's worth doing properly

We've helped IT consultancies through both the application and the call-off stages, and the pattern holds every time: the businesses that treat their G-Cloud presence as an ongoing piece of marketing, kept current and specific, consistently outperform the ones who listed themselves once and hoped. If you're applying for the first time, or your listing has gone quiet, it's worth a proper look before the next renewal window closes.

title: A Guide to RM6277 for Recruitment Agencies
author_bio: Philip has over 24 years of recruitment experience and has provided specialist bid, proposal and tender writing services for the last 14 years, across frameworks including Crown Commercial Service, Workforce Alliance and HTE.
excerpt: Ask ten recruitment agencies which public sector framework actually matters and most will say RM6277 before anything else. Here's what it covers, and where most agencies lose ground once they're on it.
body:
Ask ten recruitment agencies which public sector framework actually matters and most of them will say RM6277 before anything else. It's the Crown Commercial Service's Non-Clinical Staffing framework, and if you supply temporary or permanent staff into the NHS or wider public sector, getting onto it properly is usually worth more than any single tender you could chase on the open market.

What RM6277 actually covers

RM6277 is the current Crown Commercial Service agreement for sourcing non-clinical staff: admin, estates, corporate, facilities and operational roles, as distinct from the clinical and nursing frameworks that sit alongside it. NHS trusts and a wide range of public bodies use it to procure both temporary and permanent staffing without running a full open tender for every requirement.

Like most CCS frameworks, it's structured into lots, typically split by role category and region, and suppliers are awarded onto the specific lots that match what they actually recruit for. Being on the framework doesn't mean you're eligible for every vacancy a trust posts, only the lots you successfully applied against, so the application stage is where you decide your own ceiling for years to come.

Getting onto it versus winning through it

Same lesson as every framework I've worked on: the application and the ongoing competition for work are two entirely different exercises. Applying is a one-off event, usually with a fixed window that doesn't reopen for a long time once it closes. Winning call-offs happens continuously, through direct award for smaller or more standard requirements and mini-competition for larger or more complex ones, and that's where most of the real value sits over the life of the framework.

Agencies that treat the application as the finish line usually plateau. The ones that treat it as the starting gun, and build a genuine process for responding fast and well to call-offs, are the ones still winning three years in.

What buyers are actually scoring

Mini-competition responses on RM6277 get evaluated the same way any public sector tender does: against a published scoring matrix, usually weighted toward quality and delivery capability as much as rate. Buyers want evidence you can actually fill the roles you're bidding to supply, not just a lower day rate than the next agency on the lot. Fill rates, time to shortlist, candidate retention and your track record on comparable public sector placements all carry real weight, and vague claims about "a strong candidate network" score badly against an evaluator who has read the same sentence from six other suppliers that week.

Where agencies lose ground

Three things I see repeatedly. First, treating every mini-competition invitation the same regardless of fit, which burns capacity on opportunities you were never going to win and makes your response quality slip on the ones you should have focused on. Second, letting compliance evidence go stale: insurance certificates, right-to-work processes, safeguarding policies, all of which get checked and all of which can quietly disqualify a strong response if they've lapsed. Third, not updating your own capability evidence as your business grows, so a response written against your capacity from two years ago undersells what you can actually deliver now.

Is it worth the effort to apply

If a meaningful share of your current or target client base is NHS or wider public sector, yes, almost without exception. The application itself takes real work: proper evidence of financial standing, service descriptions written the way an evaluator reads rather than the way you'd pitch a private client, and a realistic view of which lots you can actually resource. But the agencies we've supported onto RM6277 and similar frameworks consistently describe it as the single biggest unlock in their public sector pipeline, not because it guarantees work, but because it's the gate you have to be through before any of the real competition even starts.

If you're weighing up whether to apply, or you're already on the framework and want a second opinion on why your mini-competition win rate isn't where it should be, that's exactly the conversation we have with clients every week.

title: How to Write a Tender: A Complete UK Guide
author_bio: Philip has over 24 years of recruitment experience and has provided specialist bid, proposal and tender writing services for the last 14 years, across frameworks including Crown Commercial Service, Workforce Alliance and HTE.
excerpt: Most guides to writing a tender tell you to be clear and proofread carefully, then stop. This one covers PQQ vs ITT, how evaluators actually score responses, and what wins or loses marks on social value and compliance.
body:
Most guides to writing a tender read like they were written by someone who has never sat on the other side of the table. They tell you to "be clear" and "proofread carefully" and leave it there. That advice isn't wrong, it's just not enough to win anything.

This guide is longer and more specific than most because tendering rewards specificity. We write and review UK public sector tenders for a living, across recruitment and staffing frameworks and IT consultancy frameworks including G-Cloud and DOS 7, and we've built this guide the way we'd want a client to understand the process before their first bid, not after their fifth loss.

What Is a Tender?

A tender is a formal, structured offer submitted in response to a buyer's published requirement, setting out how a supplier would deliver a contract and at what price. In the UK public sector, tenders are published because public money is involved, and procurement law requires transparent, fair competition above certain financial thresholds.

You'll see tenders referred to by several names depending on the stage and the buyer: an Invitation to Tender (ITT), a Request for Quotation (RFQ), a call-off under a framework agreement, or simply "the opportunity." They all share the same basic shape: a specification of what's needed, instructions on how to respond, and a method for scoring the responses against each other.

Public sector tenders in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland above the relevant thresholds are published on Find a Tender (the UK's replacement for the EU's OJEU system) and on Contracts Finder for lower-value opportunities, alongside buyer-specific portals. Hawkeye runs a free, daily-updated tender board that aggregates live opportunities from these sources, which is worth bookmarking before you read any further — most of what follows only matters once you've actually found something worth bidding for.

PQQ vs ITT: Understanding the Stages

Two acronyms cause more confusion than anything else in UK tendering, so it's worth being precise about them.

PQQ (Pre-Qualification Questionnaire), now more commonly called an SQ (Selection Questionnaire) since the standardised form was introduced, is the qualification gate. It asks whether your business is capable of delivering the contract at all: financial standing, insurance levels, relevant experience, technical capacity, policies on health and safety, equality, data protection and modern slavery. It is almost always scored on a pass/fail basis rather than a sliding scale. Get it wrong and you never reach the ITT, regardless of how good your actual proposal would have been.

ITT (Invitation to Tender) is the substantive competition. This is where you make the case for why your business should win, not just whether you're allowed to compete. It covers quality questions (method statements, case studies, social value, mobilisation plans) and the price. This is scored comparatively against every other bidder, usually on a weighted points system.

Not every procurement uses both stages. Lower-value or single-stage procurements combine qualification and quality questions into one document. Framework call-offs, including most G-Cloud and DOS work, typically skip a formal PQQ entirely because qualification already happened when you joined the framework — more on that later.

The Go/No-Go Decision

The best tender response in the world doesn't help if you shouldn't have bid in the first place. Before anyone writes a word, ask:

  • Can we actually deliver this? Mobilisation timescales, geographic coverage, headcount and specialist accreditations all need to be realistic, not aspirational.
  • Do we have a genuine chance? An incumbent supplier with a strong track record, a price point you can't match, or a specification written around a competitor's exact service model are all signs worth weighing honestly.
  • Is the opportunity worth the cost of bidding? A well-written ITT response for a complex contract can take many days of senior staff time. That's a real cost whether you win or not.
  • Does it fit where the business is going? Winning a contract you don't actually want, in a sector or geography you're trying to move away from, is a worse outcome than not bidding.

A good bid-no bid process is written down, not a gut feeling, and it's applied consistently even when a deadline is tight and the temptation is to bid on everything that lands. Scanning live opportunities on a tender board early, rather than discovering a contract three days before submission, gives you the time to make this decision properly instead of by default.

Reading and Interpreting the Tender Pack

Once you've decided to bid, resist the urge to start writing. Read the entire pack first — all of it, not just the questions.

A typical ITT pack includes:

  • Instructions to tenderers, covering format, word limits, submission deadline and method, and the clarification process.
  • Specification or scope of requirements, describing what the buyer actually needs delivered.
  • Evaluation methodology, setting out how marks are awarded (covered in detail below).
  • Pricing schedule, usually a fixed spreadsheet template that must not be altered.
  • Draft contract terms, which matter more than most bidders treat them — if a term is unworkable for your business, the time to raise it is during the clarification window, not after you've won.
  • SQ/PQQ responses, where applicable, plus supporting certificates (insurance, accreditations, policies).

Read for language, not just content. "Shall" and "must" signal mandatory requirements; "should" and "may" signal preference. A tender that says the supplier "must" hold a specific accreditation is telling you that missing it is a disqualifying gap, not a minor weakness to explain away.

Use the clarification process. Buyers publish a deadline for questions and circulate anonymised answers to all bidders, which then become part of the tender documentation. If something in the specification is ambiguous, ask — guessing wrong is far more expensive than asking a question that makes you look thorough.

Understanding Scoring Criteria and Evaluation Models

This is the section most guides skip, and it's the one that actually determines whether you win.

Quality and price weighting. Public sector tenders state, usually in the ITT's opening pages, what proportion of the overall score is quality versus price — commonly splits like 70/30, 60/40 or 80/20 depending on how commoditised the service is. If quality is weighted at 70%, a response that's technically compliant but thinly written against a 30% price weighting will still lose to a mediocre price backed by a strong quality submission. Know your split before you allocate a single hour of writing time, and weight your effort to match it.

Scoring descriptors. Most evaluators mark against a defined scale, typically something like 0–5 or 0–10, with written descriptors attached to each band: a 0 for no response or non-compliant, a low-middle score for a response that meets the minimum requirement but adds nothing, and the top band reserved for responses that are fully compliant, evidenced, and demonstrate genuine added value or innovation. If the buyer has published these descriptors (and under UK transparency requirements, they usually have), read them literally. "Meets requirement" and "exceeds requirement" are not the same mark, and vague confidence won't bridge that gap — specific, evidenced detail will.

Pass/fail gates. Separate from the scored quality questions, many tenders include mandatory minimum requirements: a minimum score on a specific question (common for health and safety or safeguarding), or a straightforward compliance check (insurance level, accreditation, financial standing). Fail one of these and your score on everything else becomes irrelevant. Identify every gate in the pack before you write anything else.

Moderation and consensus scoring. In most public sector evaluations, more than one evaluator scores each submission independently, then the panel moderates scores together to reach a consensus. This matters because it means your response needs to be clear enough to score consistently well with a panel of readers who weren't in the room when you wrote it, not just persuasive to one sympathetic reader.

MEAT and MAT. You'll often see the term MEAT — Most Economically Advantageous Tender — used to describe the overall evaluation approach of balancing quality and price rather than awarding on lowest price alone. Since the Procurement Act 2023 reforms, the terminology in parts of the public sector has shifted toward MAT, Most Advantageous Tender, reflecting a broader view of value that can include social and environmental factors alongside cost. The underlying principle hasn't changed: price is rarely the only, or even the main, factor.

Building a Response Plan

Write a plan before you write a word of the actual response.

  1. Deconstruct every question. Multi-part questions are common, and evaluators mark against every part. If a question asks how you'll manage mobilisation, staff training, and contingency for staff absence, your answer needs three clearly identifiable sections, not one that quietly merges them.
  2. Allocate word count to marks, not to how much you have to say. A question worth 5% of the overall score doesn't need the same word count as one worth 20%, however much more comfortable you are writing about it.
  3. Assign ownership and deadlines. Every question needs one accountable owner, even if several people contribute content, otherwise nobody takes responsibility for the final draft.
  4. Build in review stages. A first draft, a technical/content review, and a final compliance check are the minimum. The person who wrote the answer is the worst person to catch what's missing from it.
  5. Work backwards from the submission deadline, and build in slack for portal upload issues, which happen far more often than anyone expects, and are never accepted as an excuse for a late submission.

Writing to Win: Win Themes, Evidence and Language

Decide your win themes before you write. A win theme is the two or three core reasons this buyer should choose you, repeated consistently (not word-for-word, but thematically) across every answer. Without them, a multi-author bid reads like twelve separate essays rather than one coherent argument.

Evidence beats assertion, every time. "We have a strong track record" scores nothing. "We delivered 94% of placements within the contracted turnaround time on a comparable NHS workforce contract" gives the evaluator something specific and comparable to score. If you don't have a strong number for something, say what you do have honestly — a modest, evidenced claim consistently outscores a vague, impressive-sounding one, because evaluators have read enough generic bids to be suspicious of confidence that isn't backed up.

Mirror the question's own language. If the question asks about "continuity of service during staff absence," use that exact phrase early in your answer. Evaluators working through dozens of submissions against a checklist read more carefully, and score more generously, when a response visibly tracks the question rather than making them hunt for the relevant part.

Write for a tired reader. Short paragraphs, clear subheadings that match the question structure, bullet points for discrete lists, and diagrams or process maps where they genuinely clarify something. Evaluators are reading many submissions in a short window; density is not the same as depth.

Use plain English. Jargon and padding ("leveraging synergistic best-practice methodologies") read as a way of avoiding specifics, not demonstrating expertise. The strongest answers are often the plainest.

Social Value: Getting It Right

Social value is where most competitor guidance stays shallow, and where UK public sector bids are frequently won or lost on the margins.

Since the Public Services (Social Value) Act 2012, and reinforced through subsequent government procurement policy, public sector buyers are required to consider the broader social, economic and environmental benefit a contract can deliver, not just the core service. Many central government contracts formally weight social value as part of the scored quality criteria, and local authorities and NHS bodies increasingly do the same.

The common social value themes you'll see in a specification are:

  • Tackling economic inequality — local employment, apprenticeships, skills development, and supply chain opportunities for SMEs and voluntary sector organisations.
  • Fighting climate change — carbon reduction commitments tied to the actual delivery of the contract, not generic company-wide policy.
  • Equal opportunity — removing barriers to employment for disadvantaged groups, including care leavers, ex-offenders, veterans and people with disabilities.
  • Wellbeing — community engagement, health outcomes, and support for employee and community welfare.

Where most bids go wrong on social value: they submit the same generic CSR paragraph, lightly edited, in every bid they write. Evaluators who assess multiple submissions from the same market spot recycled social value content immediately, and it scores accordingly — because it demonstrates nothing specific to this contract, this buyer, or this community.

What scores well: commitments that are specific, measurable, and genuinely deliverable within the contract's scope and value. Naming the actual number of apprenticeship places you'll create on this contract, the specific local organisations you'll partner with, or the measurable training hours you'll deliver to the buyer's own workforce, beats a page of aspirational statements every time. It also helps to check whether the buyer has published their own corporate or social value strategy — aligning your commitments to their stated priorities, rather than your own generic ones, signals you've actually read their organisation, not just their tender. And because buyers increasingly track delivery against social value commitments post-award, don't promise anything you can't actually report against once you've won.

For recruitment businesses specifically, social value commitments around routes into employment for disadvantaged groups carry particular weight, since the service itself is about employment. For IT and digital suppliers, digital skills outreach, apprenticeships and STEM engagement tend to land best, because they connect directly to the sector's own expertise.

Compliance and Common Mistakes That Lose Marks

Most losing bids aren't badly written — they're non-compliant, incomplete, or careless in ways that are entirely avoidable. In order of how often we see them cost real marks:

  1. Missing mandatory documents or certificates. Insurance certificates, accreditations, policy documents — if the pack lists them as required, their absence is noticed immediately and often scored as an automatic fail on that section.
  2. Exceeding word, page or character limits. Portals increasingly enforce this automatically, cutting your answer off mid-sentence. Where it isn't enforced automatically, evaluators are instructed to stop reading at the limit, which is just as damaging.
  3. Not answering every part of a multi-part question. Evaluators mark against each identifiable sub-requirement; a strong answer to two of three parts still scores as incomplete.
  4. Generic or recycled content. Reused paragraphs from a previous bid, with the client name swapped, read exactly like what they are.
  5. Unsubstantiated claims. Confident language without evidence behind it invites scepticism rather than reassurance.
  6. Altering the pricing schedule format. Buyers usually mandate a fixed spreadsheet structure specifically so bids are comparable; reformatting it, even to make it clearer, risks disqualification.
  7. Inconsistent formatting and sloppy presentation. Mismatched fonts, broken numbering, and inconsistent terminology across sections signal a bid assembled under pressure rather than managed properly — which is exactly the impression you don't want to give a buyer who's assessing your ability to manage their contract.
  8. Late submission. Procurement portals do not grant grace periods. A submission one minute late is treated identically to one not submitted at all.

Writing Tenders for Public Sector Recruitment Contracts

Recruitment and staffing tendering has its own specific pressure points that generic tender-writing advice doesn't cover.

Workforce mobilisation and TUPE are usually central to the evaluation, particularly on contracts replacing an incumbent supplier. Buyers want a detailed, credible plan for transferring or onboarding staff without disrupting service continuity — vague reassurance here is one of the fastest ways to lose marks on an otherwise strong bid.

KPI and SLA structures in recruitment contracts typically centre on fill rates, time-to-hire, staff retention and continuity of service during absence. Your method statement needs to show how you'll actually hit these, not just that you're aware they exist.

Safeguarding, vetting and compliance (DBS checks, right-to-work verification, sector-specific registration requirements) are frequently pass/fail gates rather than scored questions — treat them with the same seriousness as a mandatory accreditation.

Social value in recruitment tenders tends to focus on routes into employment: apprenticeships, work placements for disadvantaged groups, and local labour market engagement, which connect naturally to what a recruitment business already does.

This is one of Hawkeye's core specialisms — see our bid writing service and recruitment sector guidance for more detail on how these contracts are specifically evaluated.

Writing Tenders for IT and Digital Frameworks: G-Cloud and DOS 7

IT consultancy and digital tendering largely runs through Crown Commercial Service frameworks rather than open market ITTs, and the process is structurally different.

G-Cloud is a framework for buying cloud hosting, software and support services through the Digital Marketplace. Getting listed requires an initial application, but the real tendering happens at the call-off stage, when individual public sector buyers run a further competition among listed suppliers for their specific requirement — usually with shorter, tightly word-limited written answers rather than a full ITT pack.

DOS 7 (Digital Outcomes and Specialists) covers outcomes-based digital services and individual specialist roles, evaluated per-opportunity once you're on the framework. Because there's typically no PQQ at call-off stage (qualification already happened when you joined the framework), the entire competition rests on how well you answer a small number of quality questions, often under strict word counts. That compresses everything this guide covers into less space, which makes precision and evidence density more important, not less.

Common pitfalls specific to this space: generic case studies that don't map to the specific outcome being procured, insufficient detail on specialist role alignment (particularly where SFIA levels are referenced), and underestimating how much buyers scrutinise agile delivery credibility and alignment with the Government Service Standard.

See our bid writing service and IT sector guidance for more on how we approach G-Cloud and DOS 7 responses specifically.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is the difference between a PQQ and an ITT?
A: A PQQ (Pre-Qualification Questionnaire), now usually called an SQ (Selection Questionnaire), checks whether your business is capable of delivering the contract and is typically scored pass/fail. An ITT (Invitation to Tender) is the full competitive stage where your proposal is scored against other bidders on quality and price.

Q: How long does it take to write a tender response?
A: It depends on the size and complexity of the opportunity, but most ITT responses take between five and fifteen working days from kickoff to a final, reviewed draft. Framework call-offs with short word limits can take less time, but still require the same depth of planning.

Q: What does quality and price weighting mean?
A: It's the proportion of the overall score allocated to your written quality response versus your price. A 70/30 split means your quality submission is worth more than twice as much to the final score as your price, so your writing effort should be weighted accordingly.

Q: Do I have to include social value in my response?
A: If the tender asks for it, yes, and it is almost always a scored section in UK public sector contracts rather than optional. Generic corporate social responsibility content scores poorly; specific, measurable commitments tied to the actual contract score well.

Q: What happens if I miss a mandatory requirement in the SQ?
A: Mandatory SQ requirements are usually scored pass/fail. Missing one typically disqualifies you from proceeding to the ITT stage, regardless of how strong your actual proposal would have been.

Q: Can I submit a tender after the deadline if I have a good reason?
A: No. Procurement portals do not grant grace periods, and a late submission by even a minute is almost always rejected outright. Build in time for portal issues well before the deadline.

Q: What is G-Cloud and how is bidding for it different from a normal tender?
A: G-Cloud is a Crown Commercial Service framework for buying cloud hosting, software and support services through the Digital Marketplace. Once listed, individual opportunities are won through shorter, word-limited competitions run by buyers rather than a full open-market ITT process.

Q: Do you guarantee a tender win?
A: No ethical bid writing company can guarantee a win, because the decision is made by the buyer, not the writer. What a properly planned, evidenced and compliant submission guarantees is the strongest possible chance of success.

If you're weighing up a live opportunity right now, our tender board is updated daily, and a free consultation is the fastest way to get an honest read on your chances before you commit the time to write it.
